week.t: NASA: both ESCAPADE spacecraft complete their powered Earth flybys, 7 and 9 Nov, and are on their way to Mars
NOAA: Tropical Storm Pena, 40 mph, the only tropical cyclone on the National Hurricane Center’s maps
Science News Explores: fossil ear scans show seals evolved amphibious hearing nearly 26.7 million years ago
A*STAR: Gua-SMACS-16, a molecule that kills Candida tropicalis and largely spares three related yeasts
NASA: PROMISE, a nuclear-powered Moon rover built from Mars rover spares, to launch in late 2028
NUS: Prof Lionel Wee on chatbots raised on American English “correcting” Indian English

tiles.cap: Both Mars probes fired on time: two 9-minute burns, two days apart, and they are gone
tiles.nums: powered Earth flybys: 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 Nov about 1,000 miles up, and 6 am on Monday 9 Nov about 650 miles up
tiles.p1: NASA says both twin ESCAPADE spacecraft have completed their powered Earth flybys and are on their way to Mars. The first fired its roughly 9-minute trans-Mars injection burn at 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 November, when it was about 1,000 miles above Earth’s surface; the second did the same at 6 am Eastern on Monday 9 November (7 pm in Singapore), about 650 miles up. Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for the Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters: “This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we’ve now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days.”
tiles.p2: Why it matters: Jeff Parker of Advanced Space, the lead mission designer, says the loiter-and-flyby route “provides the flexibility to launch almost anytime and then use Earth’s gravity to get a boost to Mars” instead of waiting every two years for the planets to line up.
deep: The route

ESCAPADE launched on 13 November 2025 from Cape Canaveral, when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun. The pair spent about a year in a loiter orbit around Lagrange point 2, about a million miles from Earth, then swung back past Earth so that its gravity plus the engine burn could throw them towards Mars.
Ten months to go

The cruise to Mars takes about 10 months, with trajectory correction manoeuvres along the way. Orbit insertion burns are planned for 7 and 9 September 2027, each spacecraft firing its engine for about 11 minutes, and science operations are expected to begin in June 2028.
Two orbiters, one planet

Rob Lillis of the University of California, Berkeley, the principal investigator: “This will be the first science mission to choreograph two orbiters around Mars.” The goal is to measure how the solar wind, a million-mile-per-hour stream of material from the Sun, drives the loss of the Martian atmosphere, from two places at once.
What is aboard

Each orbiter weighs about 209 kg dry and 535 kg fuelled, and carries an electrostatic analyser from UC Berkeley, a magnetometer from NASA Goddard, a Langmuir probe from Embry-Riddle and student-built cameras from Northern Arizona University. They rode to space on the second flight of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket.
tiles.src: NASA, 9 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas): NASA’s ESCAPADE Completes Powered Earth Flybys, Now En Route to Mars · NASA ESCAPADE mission page
tiles.credit: Image: Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger, via NASA

tiles.cap: Chatbots raised on American English “correct” Indian English. An NUS dean weighs in
tiles.p1: Much of the language data that AI models learn from is American English, and NUS News reports that users in India have found chatbots “correcting” Indian English expressions as grammatical mistakes. Prof Lionel Wee, Dean of the NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences and a sociolinguist, told a panel organised by The Mandala Club on 20 October that meaning depends on context: “Table number five wants their check” or “I’ve got to wash my hair” carry more than their words. He calls himself an “AI agnostic” and urges “a healthy dose of scepticism towards AI”.
tiles.p2: Why here: a Singapore take on the Using AI lane, from a professor who researches how people actually talk.
deep: Who was there

The panel, “Lost in Translation”, was organised by The Mandala Club on 20 October 2026. Alongside Prof Wee were Rahat Kapur, co-founder and editorial director of Beyond The Boardroom, and Chathuni Uduwela, a public policy practitioner.
Comfort from a machine

Two stories from the panel: a colleague’s niece turned to a chatbot for comfort after a breakup, and a student kept using a religious chatbot app long after exams were over. Wee’s question: “Are we creating generations that are less resilient, less able to deal with setbacks and difficulties”.
Like calculators?

NUS News’ comparison: writing reduced the need to memorise, and calculators made manual calculation less necessary. Its question: as AI takes on more thinking tasks, which human skills should we keep cultivating?
Access is not enough
Wee: “Access on its own is not really meaningful if you don’t take into account the kinds of friction that people encounter”.
tiles.src: NUS News, 4 Nov 2026: Is AI changing the way we speak, think and connect with one another?

tiles.cap: Four burns, 103 minutes of firing: India’s navigation satellite is parked 36,000 km up
tiles.nums: total burn time of NVS-03’s liquid apogee motor across four manoeuvres, about 103 minutes
tiles.p1: ISRO reported on 4 November that NVS-03, placed by GSLV-F18 on 30 October at 23:51 IST into an orbit of 170.3 km by 38,080 km, has completed four orbit manoeuvres with a cumulative liquid apogee motor burn of 6,164 seconds. It now sits in a geosynchronous orbit of 35,765 km by 36,196 km, at an inclination ISRO lists as 29.98 degrees, and ISRO says the health of the satellite is normal. The first burn alone, on 31 October at 16:48 IST, lasted 2,174.8 seconds and lifted the low point of the orbit from 170 km to 5,477.6 km.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: NVS-03 is the third satellite of India’s next-generation navigation system, carrying an indigenous atomic clock and adding an L1 signal to the existing L5 and S-band signals, to serve India and a region about 1,500 km around it.
deep: Why four burns

The GSLV left NVS-03 in a long ellipse, 170.3 km at its lowest and 38,080 km at its highest. The liquid apogee motor fired four times, 6,164 seconds in all, turning that ellipse into a near-circle between 35,765 and 36,196 km up.
The clocks on board

NVS-03 carries an indigenous atomic clock alongside procured atomic clocks, and adds an L1 signal to the L5 and S-band signals the series already transmits. ISRO describes it as continuing the navigation services of the IRNSS series.
What it covers
The system’s coverage is the Indian land mass and a region extending about 1,500 km around India’s geopolitical boundary.
The rocket
GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of the GSLV, from the Second Launch Pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, delivering the satellite to a geosynchronous transfer orbit.
tiles.src: ISRO, Final orbit manoeuvring of NVS-03 spacecraft (4 Nov 2026) and Orbit manoeuvring update (31 Oct 2026) · ISRO GSLV-F18 mission page
tiles.credit: Photo: ISRO (GSLV-F18 on the launch pad)

tiles.cap: A slide-out phone keyboard. The tester typed 30 words a minute on it, 53 on glass
tiles.nums: words per minute on the Clicks keyboard vs the touchscreen in Tom’s Guide’s test; accuracy 62% vs 81%
tiles.p1: Clicks’ Power Keyboard snaps to the magnets on the back of a phone (MagSafe or Qi2) and slides out as a physical keyboard: 119.7 × 76.6 × 15.2 mm, 180 g, with a built-in 2,300 mAh battery that also tops up the phone over 5 W Qi wireless charging. TIME put it on its Best Inventions 2026 list; TIME calls the company “chockablock with BlackBerry alumni”, and says co-founder Jeffrey Gadway obsessively adjusted key curvature, row spacing and actuation points. Tom’s Guide’s Jason England typed 53 words a minute at 81% accuracy on his iPhone’s glass and 30 words a minute at 62% on the Clicks.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: it is a bet that fingers remember what thumbs forgot, and the test says they mostly do not.
deep: Inside

Bluetooth LE 5.4, pairing with up to 9 devices, three of them saved to the 1, 2 and 3 keys. By default 500 mAh of the battery is reserved for the keyboard itself. There is an adjustable LED backlight and a USB-C port, but the battery cannot charge other devices through it.
What went wrong

With the keyboard slid out the phone becomes top-heavy: “I constantly felt like it was going to somersault backward out of my hands.” The reviewer also found a “cheap-feeling plastic back” and a slide-out hinge that “feels almost distressingly loose”, called 2,300 mAh small for a power bank, and 5 W charging slow.
What worked

The keys themselves were “objectively well-made”. As a pocket Bluetooth keyboard it drove a smart TV and a PS5, and it worked with Samsung DeX and Viture glasses. Verdict: “undeniably useful”, “not for everyone”.
Price
The maker’s page says “From $139” with a $30 discount already applied; Tom’s Guide listed it at $99 when the review ran in August.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Martin Cizmar) · clicks.tech Power Keyboard spec page · Tom’s Guide, 18 Aug 2026 (Jason England)

tiles.cap: Seals hear in air and under water. No other mammal can. It began 26.7 million years ago
tiles.nums: of underwater sound reaches a human ear; water is more than 800 times denser than air
tiles.p1: Water is more than 800 times denser than air, which is why less than one percent of underwater sound reaches a human ear. Seals, sea lions and walruses, the pinnipeds, have spongy ear tissue that fills with blood when they dive, equalising pressure and carrying sound well underwater. Paleontologist James Rule of Monash University in Melbourne calls this amphibious hearing “something of a superpower”: “They are the only mammals which can do this.”
tiles.p2: Why now: Science News Explores reported the fossil ear scans on Monday; the paper appeared on 15 July in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
deep: 217 ears
The team made micro-CT scans of 217 ear specimens from museums around the world, covering 119 mammal species, including all 34 living pinniped species.
When it started

Amphibious hearing evolved nearly 26.7 million years ago. Puijila, an early relative, spent much of its time in water but could hear only in air; Enaliarctos is thought to be among the first fully sea-dwelling pinnipeds.
Why not otters
Sea otters make only short dives, which may explain why they never developed acute underwater hearing.
Masters of sound
Rule: “The evolution of amphibious hearing has made pinnipeds the masters of sound.” Next time your head is under water in a pool, listen: how much of the poolside noise reaches you?
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 9 Nov 2026 (Melissa Hobson): Seals long ago evolved to hear above the water, and below · Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 15 July 2026

tiles.cap: The only storm on the hurricane maps on Monday: 40 mph winds. The forecasters: “barely”
tiles.nums: maximum sustained winds (65 km/h) of Tropical Storm Pena at 11 am Hawaii time on Monday, central pressure 1004 millibars
tiles.p1: At 7 am US Eastern on Monday the US National Hurricane Center listed no tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and none in the eastern Pacific. The only one on its maps was Tropical Storm Pena in the central Pacific, about 640 miles southwest of South Point, Hawaii, moving west at 12 mph with 40 mph winds. The 11 am Hawaii-time advisory’s headline: “PENA BARELY A TROPICAL CYCLONE”.
tiles.p2: Why now: a quiet week on the hurricane maps in a year in which the northwest Pacific had 25 named storms by late October, according to NASA Earth Observatory.
deep: By the numbers

Pena was at 11.5°N 161.4°W, about 650 miles east-southeast of Johnston Island. Tropical-storm-force winds extended up to 105 miles from the centre; there were no watches or warnings, no land hazards, and little change in strength was expected.
The other ocean

NASA Earth Observatory’s 3 November feature: the northwest Pacific had 25 named storms by late October 2026. Super Typhoon In-fa was an “annular” storm, a type that makes up about 4% of western North Pacific cyclones and whose eyes average about 45 km across against a typical 25 km; Typhoon Champi’s winds reached nearly 300 km/h. NASA Goddard meteorologist Gary Partyka calls the strong El Niño a “likely contributor”.
Reading an advisory
This was advisory number 13, with the next due at 5 pm Hawaii time, six hours later. The pressure was 1004 mb (29.65 inches), and the forecaster signed it Mahoney.
tiles.src: NOAA National Hurricane Center / Central Pacific Hurricane Center, Tropical Storm Pena Advisory 13, 11 am HST Mon 9 Nov 2026 · NASA Earth Observatory, 3 Nov 2026: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
tiles.credit: Image: NOAA / NHC–CPHC, central Pacific seven-day outlook (live)

tiles.cap: Feynman’s tiny machine was meant to get free work out of jiggling air. It gets nowhere
tiles.nums: the entropy a gas gains per molecule when you let it double its volume: Feynman’s number for “more mixed up”
tiles.p1: Richard Feynman imagined a tiny axle with vanes, like a paddle wheel, in a box of gas, connected to a ratchet and pawl, a toothed wheel with a catch that lets it turn one way only. Gas molecules bang the vanes at random; the ratchet should turn the jiggle into one-way rotation and lift a flea. It fails: the pawl is tiny too, so it jiggles as well, and the chance it is bounced up at the wrong moment, letting the wheel slip back, is e^(−ε/kT), exactly the same as the chance of the vanes gathering the energy ε to climb one tooth. At a single temperature the two cancel and the wheel goes nowhere.
tiles.p2: Why it matters, in Feynman’s words: “The fact that it gets nowhere is really the fundamental deep principle on which all of thermodynamics is based.”
deep: Make it work

Keep the vanes at a temperature T1 and the ratchet colder at T2 and it does run forward. Balancing the forward and backward rates gives Q1/Q2 = T1/T2 and a work fraction of (T1 − T2)/T1, exactly Carnot’s limit for any engine. Make the ratchet hotter than the gas and it runs backwards.
A rectifier for molecules

Feynman calls the ratchet a rectifier for molecular motion, like an electrical rectifier. Maxwell’s demon, the imaginary creature who sorts fast molecules from slow ones, fails the same way: a finite demon heats up and jiggles.
Test the arrow of time

Newton’s equations work just as well with time running backwards, yet mixed gases never unmix. Feynman’s test: film two kinds of gas molecules mixing and play it in reverse: every single collision is reversible, and the film still looks obviously wrong.
Counting arrangements

Entropy is the logarithm of the number of microscopic arrangements that look the same from outside. Letting a gas double its volume at fixed temperature adds Nk ln 2, that is k ln 2 per molecule; mixing neon with argon adds the same amount.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 46: Ratchet and pawl (Caltech, feynmanlectures.caltech.edu)

tiles.cap: Your laptop screen sends out light with a hidden direction. Sunglasses and tape reveal it
tiles.nums: the twist a half-wavelength delay gives polarised light inside a strip of stretched tape
tiles.p1: LCD screens emit polarised light: the waves wobble in one direction. The Exploratorium’s Polarized-Light Mosaic uses that. Layer strips of clear packing tape on a sheet of clear plastic, sandwich it between two polarisers (two lenses from old polarising sunglasses work), hold it up to a window and turn the front polariser: the tape blazes with colours that change as you rotate. Stick tape on an LCD screen and it looks clear until you look through a polariser.
tiles.p2: Why: the stretched polymer molecules in tape make it birefringent, so light travels at two different speeds inside it, depending on which way it is polarised.
deep: Two speeds

Light polarised parallel to the stretch moves more slowly. The two components fall out of step and recombine with a rotated polarisation; thicker tape rotates it more, and a half-wavelength delay rotates it by 90 degrees.
Why colours

Each colour has its own refractive index (the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the material), so each colour is rotated by a different amount and the second polariser lets different colours through at different angles. Where two or three strips overlap you get more colours still.
Tape warning

It needs tape with a shiny, non-matte surface; the Exploratorium says “Scotch brand tape may not work”, while some inexpensive 2-inch clear packing tapes do. Test a strip between two polarisers: it works if it goes from dark to light as you rotate one of them.

tiles.cap: In 1977 a star blinked five times before Uranus hid it. That is how its rings were found
tiles.nums: dimmings before Uranus covered the star and five flickers after: one for each ring
tiles.p1: An occultation is when one object in the sky passes in front of another that looks smaller. In 1977 astronomers watched Uranus pass in front of a distant star and saw the star’s light dim five times before the planet blocked it, then flicker five times afterwards. Each dip was one of Uranus’s five rings crossing the starlight, rings that “do not glow brightly like Saturn’s”.
tiles.p2: Why here: Science News Explores’ word of the week on Monday was occultation. The Moon passes in front of stars and planets pretty much every night.
deep: The Moon as a knife-edge

Lunar occultations happen almost nightly as the Moon moves in front of stars and planets; occultations by planets are rarer. Watching starlight flicker behind the Moon can reveal its mountains and valleys.
Measuring an asteroid
Timing how long a star stays hidden behind an asteroid tells astronomers how big the asteroid is, without ever seeing its shape directly.
Alien air

When a world with an atmosphere occults a star, the starlight passes through that air on its way to us. The article puts it this way: occultations “can grant astronomers a rare opportunity to analyze a world’s atmosphere.”
The reverse
A transit is the opposite case: a smaller-looking object passing in front of a larger one, such as an exoplanet crossing the face of its star.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 9 Nov 2026 (Katie Grace Carpenter): Scientists Say: Occultation

tiles.cap: A*STAR built a molecule that kills one yeast and spares its close cousins. That is hard
tiles.nums: Candida species killed: C. tropicalis died, while C. albicans, C. auris and C. glabrata were largely spared in mixed cultures
tiles.p1: Broad-spectrum antifungal drugs kill the harmful fungus and can also kill the helpful ones living in you. A*STAR’s Infectious Diseases Labs and Bioinformatics Institute designed Gua-SMACS-16, a synthetic molecule that killed Candida tropicalis while largely sparing mammalian cells, zebrafish embryos and three related yeasts, C. albicans, C. auris and C. glabrata, in mixed cultures. Senior scientist Ning Li: “A narrow-spectrum antifungal could offer important advantages by preserving beneficial fungi in the microbiome”.
tiles.p2: Why now: published in Advanced Science and highlighted by A*STAR Research on Monday.
deep: The tell
The selectivity is linked to β-glucan, a major component of fungal cell walls: C. tropicalis walls contain relatively less β-glucan than the other species tested.
Team-up

Combined with the existing drug caspofungin, Gua-SMACS-16 showed strong synergy against other Candida species, including C. auris, which the WHO designates a critical priority. Yue Wang of A*STAR IDL: “Caspofungin reduces β-glucan production, which may weaken cell walls and allow more Gua-SMACS-16 to reach cell membranes”.
What SMACS means
Synthetic membrane-active cationic supramolecule. Wang: “Gua-SMACS-16 is designed to preferentially bind fungal cells, rather than mammalian ones”.
tiles.src: A*STAR Research, 9 Nov 2026: A targeted SMAC-down on fungal foes · Advanced Science 13 (41), 2026

tiles.cap: NASA’s next Moon rover: Mars rover spares, with a nuclear generator on its back
tiles.nums: how cold the permanently shadowed craters the rover will drive into may get (minus 400 °F)
tiles.p1: On Saturday 7 November at the MAX POWER expo at Kennedy Space Center, NASA announced PROMISE, the Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration: an SUV-sized, six-wheeled, nuclear-powered rover for the Moon’s south pole, targeted to launch in late 2028 on an 18-month mission. JPL is building it from a combination of spare flight parts and engineering test models from the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, including the electronics, body structure and mobility system of the duplicate Curiosity test-bed vehicle. Blue Origin gets a $94 million contract, with an option worth a further $140 million based on performance, to deliver it on its Mark 1 lander.
tiles.p2: Why now: the same announcement gave eight companies places on CLPS 2, a 10-year cargo-lander contract worth up to $10 billion in total, plus about $1.3 billion of launch task orders. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman: “We are building the Moon Base mission by mission.”
deep: A nuclear generator

Power comes from a flight-spare multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator, which NASA describes as essentially a nuclear generator, fitted at the rear of the rover once it reaches the launch site. It lets PROMISE work through the long lunar night and inside permanently shadowed regions, where temperatures may fall to minus 242 °C.
A drill and a dashcam

The TRIDENT drill, from Honeybee Robotics, pulls up soil from as deep as 1 metre in 10-centimetre steps. Spectrometers analyse what comes up; a radiation detector rides along whose earlier version has run for 15 years on Curiosity; and a stereo Lunar Dashcam with its own illuminators is based on Perseverance’s landing cameras.
Shackleton Crater

NASA’s PROMISE page pictures Shackleton Crater, near the Moon’s south pole, about 21 kilometres wide and 4 kilometres deep. Laser altimetry from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed boulders and low hills in its permanently shadowed interior.
For students too

On Sunday 8 November NASA opened a $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge in six categories, from power generation and construction to astronaut safety. It is for teams at US high schools and post-secondary schools, with registration by 25 January 2027.
tiles.src: NASA release 26-095, 7 Nov 2026 · NASA PROMISE mission page, updated 7 Nov 2026 · NASA release 26-096, 8 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: NASA is hiring astronauts. Last time, more than 8,000 people applied and 10 got in
tiles.nums: applicants were chosen for NASA’s 2025 astronaut class; applications for the next class opened on Saturday
tiles.p1: NASA opened applications on Saturday 7 November for its next class of astronauts, who it says will join the agency as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. US citizens have until 11:59 pm US Eastern on Thursday 3 December to submit their applications, and NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027. The agency last opened applications in 2024: from more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are now completing nearly two years of training.
tiles.p2: Why now: applications opened on Saturday 7 November and close at 11:59 pm US Eastern on Thursday 3 December; final selection is expected in late 2027, when training begins.
deep: The numbers
Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates. The agency has 32 astronauts active in its astronaut corps today.
If you want to fly it

For pilots, NASA lists 750 hours as pilot in command of high-performance jet aircraft, or 1,500 total flight hours in other fixed-wing aircraft including 750 as pilot in command, or 1,000 total flight hours in rotary-wing aircraft including 300 as pilot in command. Only US citizens can apply.
What they said

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, adding that the missions “will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage.” Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson put it shorter: “The window is open. The mission is waiting.”
Who picks

Scott Tingle, chief astronaut, chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston; for those who apply, he says, becoming a NASA astronaut “is more than a career opportunity”. The photo shows NASA announcing its 2025 astronaut candidate class at Johnson on 22 September 2025.
tiles.src: NASA news release 26-093, 7 Nov 2026 · NASA media advisory M26-084 (MAX POWER key events), updated 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Glasses with a 70° view, 1920×1200 per eye, 95 g. The computer lives in your pocket
tiles.nums: for the glasses; the tethered puck that does the computing weighs 265 g and carries a 4,455 mAh battery
tiles.p1: XREAL’s Aura, on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list, puts the computing power in a tethered puck that clips over a pocket or hangs on a lanyard, so the glasses themselves weigh 95 g. Each eye gets a Sony micro-OLED at 1920 × 1200 pixels, up to 120 Hz, with a 70-degree field of view through XREAL’s X Prism optics and electrochromic dimming in five steps. Three cameras sit on the front frame: two tracking cameras for hand tracking and spatial anchoring, and one RGB camera with a privacy LED.
tiles.p2: Why now: XREAL says shipping is expected to begin in mid-November 2026, at US$1,099 on its US store, with the US, Canada, Japan and South Korea first.
deep: The puck

It runs Android XR on a Snapdragon platform rated at 48 TOPS of AI processing, with 12 or 16 GB of memory, a fan for cooling and a 4,455 mAh rated battery. It takes Bluetooth keyboards, mice and game controllers, and has a fingerprint button.
Latency
XREAL’s X1S co-processor in the glasses is rated at 3 ms motion-to-photon latency. Brightness is rated up to 1,050 nits.
What reviewers found wrong

Tom’s Guide’s Jason England, trying them at Google I/O in May, saw “some edge blurring”, found it “slower to do things than on an actual computer”, and wrote that “you won’t be taking these outside in public without getting second looks”. He estimated the puck is “probably good for 2-3 hours of heavy use”; XREAL lists no battery life in hours.
The price problem

England: “while I’d love for these to be sub-$1,000, I don’t see a world where this happens.” TechRadar’s Hamish Hector, trying them at IFA in September, hoped for the same and noted “there’s only so cheap we can expect XR tech to get”.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Richard Eisenberg, 15 Oct 2026) · XREAL Aura specifications and US store · Tom’s Guide hands-on (Jason England, updated 21 May 2026) · TechRadar (Hamish Hector, 4 Sep 2026)

tiles.cap: Two people, one screen, different colours. Sometimes the display is at fault
tiles.nums: types of cone cell in the eye; displays mix red, green and blue to target them, but not everyone’s cones respond the same way
tiles.p1: People perceive colours differently, especially on modern displays that produce a wide range of colours, reports Physics World. Colour vision works thanks to three types of cone photoreceptor cells, and almost all display technologies exploit this by using red, green and blue. The problem with newer displays, Physics World explains, is that they do not necessarily activate the cones of different observers equally. The work was led by Andy Rider of the Institute of Ophthalmology at University College London.
tiles.p2: How it started: Rider says the work began when display technology consultant John Frith got in touch with his group, after a friend of Frith’s in the film industry saw the colours of two side-by-side cinema projectors as wildly different.
deep: Where it is published
The research was led by Andy Rider of UCL’s Institute of Ophthalmology and is published in Optics Express (DOI 10.1364/OE.613255).
The friend’s eyes

The Physics World anecdote has a twist: when Rider’s group tested the friend who saw the two projectors so differently, he turned out to have a red–green colour-vision deficiency he had not known about. Rider says he has the same condition and was not properly diagnosed until his mid-30s. Displays can drive cones unequally, and eyes differ too.
Three cones

The three cone types are called L, M and S, and each one responds to different wavelengths of visible light. When two people’s cones differ, the same red, green and blue mix on a display can look different to each of them, what Physics World calls colour mismatches, or metamerism failures.
tiles.src: Physics World, “Why do people see colours differently? Sometimes, it’s the display’s fault”, Isabelle Dumé, 5 Nov 2026 · Optics Express

tiles.cap: Eyes shut, hands up: touch your nose, then your left thumb. Now wiggle the fingers, retry
tiles.p1: Close your eyes and raise both hands above your head, keeping the fingers of your left hand completely still. With your right hand, quickly touch your right index fingertip to your nose, then to the tip of your left thumb. Go back to your nose and try each left fingertip in turn, then switch hands. The Exploratorium’s Proprioception snack asks: how accurately did you find each fingertip, did you improve, and did left and right differ? Now repeat with the fingers of the raised hand wiggling.
tiles.p2: Why wiggling helps: moving fingers feed the brain extra information about where they are, so they become easier to locate in space; repetition improves the result too.
deep: The sixth sense

Proprioceptors, also called stretch receptors, in your muscles, tendons, joints and inner ear send position information to the brain, which works out how your body is oriented and moving. Most people lean heavily on vision for position and distance, so proprioception alone gives imprecise results.
Who used it

The Exploratorium pairs the snack with Dr Patricia Cowings, a psychophysiologist who trained as a NASA astronaut, was an alternate for a 1979 spaceflight, developed individually tailored protocols to prevent motion sickness in astronauts, and is principal investigator at NASA Ames Research Center.
Two more versions
The same page has two further activities, marking an X and writing with eyes shut, which need paper and pencil. The hands-only version needs nothing at all.

tiles.cap: MIT’s phrase for what a chatbot answer can create: “the illusion of learning”
tiles.nums: principles in MIT’s 2026 report on AI in education
tiles.p1: MIT’s report does not call for banning AI. One of its eight principles is augmentation, not automation: AI should be used to “augment and enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning, not automate them.” Its named risks are the ones you would expect, weaker memory and confidence, falling back on AI at the first hint of struggle, and one you might not: fewer people. MIT saw fewer students at office hours and, anecdotally, fewer in-person groups in dorms and libraries, turning to AI instead of to classmates, TAs or professors.
tiles.p2: The point: the product of school is you, not the mark.
deep: What MIT asks of its own students
Learn to write good prompts, check every output, recognise when it has made something up, and know when not to use it at all.
Why checking matters

The report warns that models hallucinate, so students need to learn when an output is likely to be made up. MIT’s guidance for research: a human is responsible for verifying the output, and AI should never be listed as a co-author.
Keep it human

The report says every subject should include a regular in-person social component, calls for more project-based work, and asks for deliberately AI-free experiences and AI-free spaces for interaction and assessment.
tiles.src: MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training, Aug 2026
